name: Hydrogen peroxide gum rinse
lead: A hydrogen peroxide gum rinse is a diluted solution of hydrogen peroxide swished in the mouth as an antiseptic. People use it for healthier-looking pink gums, a cleaner mouth and, some say, brighter-looking teeth, all of which feed into how a smile looks. Hydrogen peroxide is also the active agent in many tooth-whitening products [1][3].

A review summarised on Wikipedia found a positive effect of dilute hydrogen peroxide over placebo for gingivitis and plaque, but concluded that chlorhexidine is far more effective [1]. Gingivitis articles list hydrogen peroxide among antiseptic rinses used for prevention and home treatment [2]. Wikipedia's mouthwash article describes peroxide as an oxidising rinse, such as a 1.5 percent product, often used short-term for acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis, that kills anaerobic bacteria and froths against debris to clean it mechanically [4].

Forum users on T Nation describe years of peroxide rinsing and report cleaner dental check-ups and whiter-looking teeth, while the mouthwash literature notes that prolonged use can enlarge the lingual papillae, the bumps on the tongue [4][5].

paras: Peroxide rinses act as oxidising antiseptics. Wikipedia says peroxide kills anaerobic bacteria and cleans mechanically as it froths against debris, and that it is used short-term for acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis [4]. Gingivitis, the mildest form of gum disease, is caused by plaque and shows as red, swollen gums that bleed easily, which is why antiseptic rinses are part of prevention and home care [2].

Mouthwashes more broadly come as antiseptic, analgesic, antifungal, anticavity and saliva-substitute types, and the American Dental Association says brushing and flossing are sufficient in most cases, with rinses as an adjunct [4]. Chlorhexidine, used at 0.05 to 0.2 percent, adheres to oral surfaces and stays active for hours, and has been known as a plaque-preventing agent since Harald Loe's work in the late 1960s [4].

Users rinse for pink, calm-looking gums, less visible plaque and fresher breath, and some for a brighter smile. A T Nation poster who began rinsing with hydrogen peroxide several years earlier says people started asking whether he had whitened his teeth, that dental cleanings often needed very little, and that his gums stay healthy; he adds that warnings against it came from people without hard science [5]. Another poster who asked about prescription chlorhexidine replies that he has used peroxide as a mouthwash for years [6], and a third describes brushing five or more times a day, flossing, and going through gallons of peroxide mouthwash [7]. These are personal accounts.

The cited review found hydrogen peroxide beneficial over placebo for plaque and gingivitis but much less effective than chlorhexidine [1]. A 2004 randomised trial supported a fluoridated hydrogen peroxide rinse for gingivitis [2]. Wikipedia's mouthwash article notes that manufacturers claim reductions in plaque, cavities, gingivitis and bad breath, and that experts generally agree rinsing does not replace brushing and flossing [4].

Peroxide whitens teeth by diffusing into the tooth and breaking down into free radicals that split pigment molecules into smaller, less pigmented pieces, so less light is absorbed [3]. Whitening gels are far more concentrated than a rinse: in-office gels typically hold 10-44% carbamide peroxide, roughly 3-16% hydrogen peroxide, and the EU limits retail products to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6% allowed under dental supervision [3]. Sensitivity is common after in-office whitening, and peroxide at 10% or higher can damage gum tissue, with poorly fitting trays a common cause of chemical burns [3].

Concentrations as low as 3% can be dangerous to the eye [1]. The FDA generally recognises hydrogen peroxide as safe as an antimicrobial agent, though this is not specific to dental use [1]. Wikipedia's mouthwash article reports that side effects can occur with prolonged use, including hypertrophy of the lingual papillae [4].

The same article lists common minor mouthwash effects as taste disturbance, tooth staining and dry mouth, notes that ingestion of some products can cause serious harm especially in young children, and reports that the possibility that antiseptic rinses disrupt the oral microbiome comes from hypothesis-generating reviews [4].

A systematic review found hydrogen peroxide rinses better than placebo for gingivitis and plaque but less effective than chlorhexidine [1], and a 2004 randomised trial supported a fluoridated hydrogen peroxide rinse [2]. No trials were found of peroxide rinsing for the look of gum colour or tooth shade.

timeline.event: Harald Loe shows that chlorhexidine can prevent plaque buildup, setting the benchmark for antiseptic rinses [4].
Randomised trial supports a fluoridated hydrogen peroxide rinse for gingivitis [2].

lore.intro: Peroxide mouthwash appears on T Nation as a long-running habit among lifters and as an alternative to prescription chlorhexidine [5][6].

claims.claim: A peroxide rinse calms inflamed gums and keeps plaque down.
claims.believers: Proponents say its antiseptic action reduces gum bacteria cheaply; one T Nation poster says gums stay healthy and cleanings need very little [5].
claims.experts: A review found benefit over placebo but chlorhexidine more effective [1].

claims.believers: A T Nation poster says people began asking if he had whitened his teeth after he started rinsing [5].
claims.experts: Peroxide is the active agent in whitening products, but those use much higher concentrations under regulation [3].

claims.claim: Peroxide can stand in for prescription mouthwash.
claims.believers: A poster who asked about chlorhexidine says he has used peroxide mouthwash for years [6].
claims.experts: The review reports chlorhexidine is far more effective than peroxide [1].

claims.believers: The T Nation poster says those who call it unhealthy cite no hard science [5].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes prolonged use can enlarge the lingual papillae, and that eye contact with 3 percent solutions can be dangerous [1][4].

card.summary: Dilute peroxide swished as a gum antiseptic; some trial support for gingivitis but chlorhexidine is reported more effective.

quick.overview:
A hydrogen peroxide rinse is a diluted solution swished in the mouth to reduce plaque and gum inflammation.

A review found it better than placebo for gingivitis but far less effective than chlorhexidine.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an antimicrobial and oxidising agent on oral bacteria and plaque.
quick.risks: Even 3% solutions can injure the eye; the FDA generally recognises peroxide as safe as an antimicrobial, not specifically for dental use.
